Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and let $y:I\to\mathbb R^d$ solve $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open interval $I$. $$|f_j(s,y(s))|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))|\le M_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$

$$g_i'(s)=\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))f_j(s,y(s)),\qquad |g_i'(s)|\le B_i.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: By [F3]–[F4], $f$ is totally differentiable and continuous on $V$, with state derivative matrix $D_yf$. On each open convex fiber $V_t$, the derivative bound and [F5]–[F6] make $f(t,\cdot)$ $L$-Lipschitz. Thus the hypotheses of [F7] hold and the IVP has a unique maximal solution; the given solution agrees with it throughout $[0,T]$.

Fix any $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ satisfying the stated compact-set condition, and fix a component $i$. Define $g_i(s):=f_i(t+s,y(t+s))$ for $0\le s\le h$. The exact path segment lies in $K\subset V$, so [F8] gives $|g_i'(s)|\le B_i$ on $(0,h)$.
For each $s\in(0,h]$, [F10] applied to $g_i$ on $[0,s]$ yields $|g_i(s)-g_i(0)|\le B_i s$; at $s=0$ the same inequality is equality.

Apply [F9] to the IVP restarted at $(t,y(t))$; then $y_i(t+h)-y_i(t)=\int_0^h g_i(s)\,ds$. Euler's output from the exact state is $y_i(t)+hg_i(0)$, so $\delta_{h,i}(t;y)=\int_0^h(g_i(0)-g_i(s))\,ds$. Using [step 2.1] gives $|\delta_{h,i}(t;y)|\le\int_0^h B_i s\,ds=B_i h^2/2$. Squaring the component bounds, summing, and using [F11] gives the asserted Euclidean norm estimate. Its constant is independent of $t$ and $h$, proving uniform local order one under [F1].

For any admitted $t\in[0,T]$, $h>0$, and $u,v\in V_t$, [F3] identifies the derivative of $z\mapsto f(t,z)$ with $D_yf(t,z)$; [F5]–[F6] give $\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2$. Therefore [F12] gives $\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2+h\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$, which is the one-step stability bound in [F1] for inputs in $K$.

$$g_i'(s)=\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))f_j(s,y(s)),\qquad |g_i'(s)|\le B_i.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: By [F3]–[F4], $f$ is totally differentiable and continuous on $V$, with state derivative matrix $D_yf$. On each open convex fiber $V_t$, the derivative bound and [F5]–[F6] make $f(t,\cdot)$ $L$-Lipschitz. Thus the hypotheses of [F7] hold and the IVP has a unique maximal solution; the given solution agrees with it throughout $[0,T]$.

Fix any $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ satisfying the stated compact-set condition, and fix a component $i$. Define $g_i(s):=f_i(t+s,y(t+s))$ for $0\le s\le h$. The exact path segment lies in $K\subset V$, so [F8] gives $|g_i'(s)|\le B_i$ on $(0,h)$.
For each $s\in(0,h]$, [F10] applied to $g_i$ on $[0,s]$ yields $|g_i(s)-g_i(0)|\le B_i s$; at $s=0$ the same inequality is equality.

Apply [F9] to the IVP restarted at $(t,y(t))$; then $y_i(t+h)-y_i(t)=\int_0^h g_i(s)\,ds$. Euler's output from the exact state is $y_i(t)+hg_i(0)$, so $\delta_{h,i}(t;y)=\int_0^h(g_i(0)-g_i(s))\,ds$. Using [step 2.1] gives $|\delta_{h,i}(t;y)|\le\int_0^h B_i s\,ds=B_i h^2/2$. Squaring the component bounds, summing, and using [F11] gives the asserted Euclidean norm estimate. Its constant is independent of $t$ and $h$, proving uniform local order one under [F1].

For any admitted $t\in[0,T]$, $h>0$, and $u,v\in V_t$, [F3] identifies the derivative of $z\mapsto f(t,z)$ with $D_yf(t,z)$; [F5]–[F6] give $\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2$. Therefore [F12] gives $\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2+h\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$, which is the one-step stability bound in [F1] for inputs in $K$.

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Under the smoothness and compact-tube hypotheses of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]], the forward Euler, explicit midpoint, and classical four-stage tableaus of [[def-euler-midpoint-rk4-tableaus]] have uniform local orders at least one, two, and four, respectively.

For the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, set $z=h\lambda$. The corresponding stability functions, defined by $y^+=R(z)y$, are
$$R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z,\qquad R_{\mathrm M}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2},\qquad R_{\mathrm{RK4}}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}+\frac{z^3}{6}+\frac{z^4}{24}.$$
The absolute stability region of a listed method is $\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\le1\}$. On the negative real axis, the Euler and midpoint regions are exactly $[-2,0]$. No maximal real interval is asserted here for RK4.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For every real $x$,

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. $$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

derivations.claim: The row sums of each $A$ in [F1] are its displayed vector $c$, so all three are explicit tableaux in the required convention [F4].
Euler has $\sum b_i=1$. Midpoint has $\sum b_i=1$ and $\sum b_ic_i=1/2$. These are the order-one and order-two equations of [F2].

For classical RK4 the row-sum vector is $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$, and direct row multiplication gives $Ac=(0,0,1/4,1/2)$, $Ac^{[2]}=(0,0,1/8,1/4)$, and $A^2c=(0,0,0,1/4)$. Therefore $\sum b_i=1$, $\sum b_ic_i=1/2$, $\sum b_ic_i^2=1/3$, $\sum b_i(Ac)_i=1/6$, $\sum b_ic_i^3=1/4$, $\sum b_i(Ac^{[2]})_i=1/12$, $\sum b_ic_i(Ac)_i=1/8$, and $\sum b_i(A^2c)_i=1/24$.

Complexify the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$. Euler multiplies $y$ by $1+z$. Midpoint has $k_1=\lambda y$ and $k_2=\lambda(y+\frac h2k_1)$, so its output factor is $1+z+\frac12z^2$. For RK4 the successive slopes are $\lambda y$, $\lambda y(1+z/2)$, $\lambda y(1+z/2+z^2/4)$, and $\lambda y(1+z+z^2/2+z^3/4)$; weighting them by $(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$ gives the displayed fourth-degree polynomial.
Apply [F2] to the sums in steps 1.2 and 1.3. It gives the asserted local orders for Euler, midpoint, and classical RK4 under exactly the hypotheses of that proposition.

For real $z$, $|1+z|\le1$ is equivalent to $-2\le z\le0$. Also $R_{\mathrm M}(z)=\frac12((z+1)^2+1)>0$, so $|R_{\mathrm M}(z)|\le1$ is equivalent to $(z+1)^2\le1$, again $z\in[-2,0]$. This proves the two stated scalar intervals.

The local-order statements concern exact-start defects; the stability functions concern boundedness on the scalar linear test equation. The finite intervals just computed give the explicit stability restriction $h\rho\le2$ for $y'=-\rho y$ with $\rho>0$; they assert neither nonlinear contractivity nor a matrix bound for nonnormal systems.

Input: levels $\ell=0,\ldots,L$ with $L\ge1$; fine-grid systems $A_\ell u_\ell=b_\ell$ of the form in [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]]; coarsening factors $m_\ell\ge2$ dividing $N_\ell$ with $N_{\ell+1}=N_\ell/m_\ell$; transfers $P_\ell,R_\ell$ from the F/C construction in [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]]; and pre/post-relaxations selected from its F- and FCF-relaxations. At each level $\ell<L$, form the practical coarse matrix $A_{\ell+1}$ with identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_{\ell,j}$ as in [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]]. Each noncoarsest level has a positive integer recursive visit count $\nu_\ell$. Also supply an initial fine-level iterate, a chosen norm on the fine-level residual space as in [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], outer cycle budget $J_{\rm out}\ge0$, and residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. The hierarchy must provide a nonsingular coarse system at every level and an exact solve on level $L$. V-cycles use $\nu_\ell=1$ and W-cycles use $\nu_\ell=2$. This algorithm gives no existence or convergence claim for a hierarchy that fails these input conditions.

For a recursive call at level $\ell$, perform the following operations on an initial guess $u_\ell$:
1. If $\ell=L$, solve $A_Lu_L=b_L$ exactly by forward substitution and return.
2. Apply the selected pre-relaxation to $A_\ell u_\ell=b_\ell$; compute $r_\ell=b_\ell-A_\ell u_\ell$ and restrict it to $r_{\ell+1}=R_\ell r_\ell$.
3. Set the coarse correction $z_{\ell+1}=0$. Repeat $\nu_\ell$ times: form $\rho_{\ell+1}=r_{\ell+1}-A_{\ell+1}z_{\ell+1}$; recursively apply the level $\ell+1$ cycle to $A_{\ell+1}\delta_{\ell+1}=\rho_{\ell+1}$ from zero initial correction; then set $z_{\ell+1}\leftarrow z_{\ell+1}+\delta_{\ell+1}$.
4. Correct $u_\ell\leftarrow u_\ell+P_\ell z_{\ell+1}$ and apply the selected post-relaxation.

Return the updated fine-level vector when the call completes. At level $0$, check the residual before the first outer cycle and after every completed cycle; return status converged only when the residual tolerance is met. After $J_{\rm out}$ cycles without a verified residual certificate, return the last iterate with status budget-exhausted. Inexact level solves contribute explicit update defects; no such defect is hidden in the exact-arithmetic cycle.

No two-grid contraction is transferred to this recursive cycle; convergence requires a bound for its actual full recursive error operator.

For the literal operations of [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]], put $N_f=N$ and $N_c=N/m$. One F-relaxation uses $N_f-N_c-1$ fine-propagator calls; one C-relaxation uses $N_c$; and one FCF-relaxation uses $2(N_f-N_c-1)+N_c$. The specified coarse forward substitution uses $N_c$ practical coarse-propagator applications, including the evaluation at $z_0=0$. These counts concern completed operations without eliminating calls at zero inputs.

In an additive accounting model with nonnegative call costs $c_\Phi,c_\Psi$, the modeled work is $n_\Phi c_\Phi+n_\Psi c_\Psi+\kappa$, where $n_\Phi,n_\Psi$ count all executed calls and $\kappa$ accounts for all remaining work. Residuals, restriction, interpolation and stopping checks must contribute their actual calls and overhead; cached values incur no new call. A parallel schedule must respect the serial order within each F-interval and in the coarse solve, and its communication and synchronization. No measured speedup is asserted.

The delegated Schur calls retain their specified rounded arithmetic, admissible input representations, range conditions and statuses; their returned factors remain candidates until the exact checks below succeed.

The default real-block sign controller is the fixed exact real-arithmetic expression tree $s=(a-d)^2+4bc$, followed by its sign comparisons, for [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]]. This uses five exact arithmetic operations and at most two sign comparisons in the declared exact local arithmetic model. For rational/dyadic encoded stored values, [[lem-exact-rational-two-by-two-discriminant-sign]] gives the finite exact integer realization; a fixed-format decoder, when used, is included in the control cost. These exact controller operations are separate from the rounded Schur matrix updates. No bit-complexity bound for integer/rational arithmetic is claimed.

Choose either bounded-controller mode, the default, or arbitrary-terminating-controller mode. In bounded mode supply a nonnegative integer per-call budget $K$. Custom sign or decoding routines are finite instruction programs over exact scalar real/integer arithmetic, comparisons, register operations and branches; no opaque callback is a unit instruction. The interpreter charges one unit per executed instruction, including decoding, the built-in tree and any custom-result verification within the same per-call $K$ budget; it checks instruction/operation validity when encountered and returns undecided on exhaustion or invalid execution. An undecided sign is propagated as the Schur type-undecided status and then outer `schur-failure`. The fixed built-in sign tree or integer recipe has a fixed finite instruction count independent of matrix dimension. Any custom reported sign must agree with the built-in exact discriminant tree before acceptance. In arbitrary-terminating mode custom programs must terminate on every supplied input; record their total executed controller work as $C_{\rm aux}$. derivations.claim: Hessenberg reduction uses at most $\max(n-2,0)$ reflector steps. For $n\ge3$, forming one reflector costs $O(n)$ scalar operations, and applying its two-sided similarity to the remaining dense submatrix costs $O(n^2)$; summing over at most $n$ steps gives $O(n^3)$. Any full initialization zero-pattern checks also cost at most $O(n^2)$ per stage, hence at most $O(n^3)$ in total. For $n=1,2$, there are no such reflector stages and no below-subdiagonal entries.

For an active block of size $r\ge2$, a Francis sweep has at most $\max(r-2,0)+1$ initial/chase reflectors of length two or three. Each acts on a bounded number of rows and columns across at most $n$ entries. For a processed interval $[a,b]$ of length $r$, every matrix write has a row or column in that interval. Before the chase, initialization or the preceding accepted check has established that the complementary below-subdiagonal positions are zero. The prescribed post-block check enumerates only the positions touching this interval: at most $nr$ in its rows and $nr$ in its columns, plus the $n$ row-loop visits. It is therefore equivalent to the full Hessenberg check and costs $O(nr)$, since every active interval has $r\ge2$. The disjoint active lengths sum to at most $n$, so all these checks cost $O(n^2)$ per sweep, even if every polynomial vector is zero and all factors are identities. The explicit partition/deflation passes and direct shift-table lookups also fit within $O(n^2)$; for $n=1$ there is no active sweep. Thus a full sweep, including all non-controller status work, costs $O(n^2)$. The linear sweep budgets therefore give $O(n^3)$ matrix work for the two Schur calls. A range, breakdown, invariant, budget, missing-shift or unavailable-sign failure stops within these bounded loops and adds only its partial-output work; it cannot increase their worst-case count. The same bound covers materializing the recorded factor products: initialization contributes $O(n^3)$ and each bounded-support chase factor updates only a bounded number of dense-factor columns, at cost $O(n)$.

derivations.claim: Hessenberg reduction uses at most $\max(n-2,0)$ reflector steps. For $n\ge3$, forming one reflector costs $O(n)$ scalar operations, and applying its two-sided similarity to the remaining dense submatrix costs $O(n^2)$; summing over at most $n$ steps gives $O(n^3)$. Any full initialization zero-pattern checks also cost at most $O(n^2)$ per stage, hence at most $O(n^3)$ in total. For $n=1,2$, there are no such reflector stages and no below-subdiagonal entries.

For an active block of size $r\ge2$, a Francis sweep has at most $\max(r-2,0)+1$ initial/chase reflectors of length two or three. Each acts on a bounded number of rows and columns across at most $n$ entries. For a processed interval $[a,b]$ of length $r$, every matrix write has a row or column in that interval. Before the chase, initialization or the preceding accepted check has established that the complementary below-subdiagonal positions are zero. The prescribed post-block check enumerates only the positions touching this interval: at most $nr$ in its rows and $nr$ in its columns, plus the $n$ row-loop visits. It is therefore equivalent to the full Hessenberg check and costs $O(nr)$, since every active interval has $r\ge2$. The disjoint active lengths sum to at most $n$, so all these checks cost $O(n^2)$ per sweep, even if every polynomial vector is zero and all factors are identities. The explicit partition/deflation passes and direct shift-table lookups also fit within $O(n^2)$; for $n=1$ there is no active sweep. Thus a full sweep, including all non-controller status work, costs $O(n^2)$. The linear sweep budgets therefore give $O(n^3)$ matrix work for the two Schur calls. A range, breakdown, invariant, budget, missing-shift or unavailable-sign failure stops within these bounded loops and adds only its partial-output work; it cannot increase their worst-case count. The same bound covers materializing the recorded factor products: initialization contributes $O(n^3)$ and each bounded-support chase factor updates only a bounded number of dense-factor columns, at cost $O(n)$.

Each exact Schur-certificate matrix product, the transform $U^*CV$, and the final transform $UYV^*$ cost $O(n^3)$. The block substitution has at most $n^2$ block pairs; each pair sums at most $O(n)$ earlier blocks of bounded size and solves a system of dimension at most four, so all substitution work is $O(n^3)$.

Each sweep checks at most $O(n)$ active blocks, and initialization and final checks add at most $O(n)$ such calls. With $O(n)$ sweeps there are at most $O(n^2)$ sign/representation-controller calls. A bounded call executes at most $K$ instructions, giving $O(Kn^2)$ work; the fixed built-in exact polynomial tree and rational/dyadic recipe are constant-size special cases. In arbitrary-terminating mode their actual total work is precisely the additional $C_{\rm aux}$.

The backward-error accumulator starts with one outward Frobenius norm of the input, costing $O(n^2)$ by the declared entrywise evaluator model. Each similarity uses a fixed number of scalar upper-bound calls once its local coefficient is evaluated. The explicit real/complex coefficient formulas require $O(m)$ scalar operations on active dimension $m$: their dimension-dependent powers can be formed by repeated multiplication and a square root for a half-integer exponent. Thus the at most $n$ initialization coefficients cost $O(n^2)$ in total, while each length-two/three chase coefficient costs $O(1)$. There are $O(n^2)$ chase similarities over the linear number of sweeps. Each recorded one-entry deflation has Frobenius norm equal to the modulus of its signed stored value, evaluated from that one-entry list with $O(1)$ scalar work; at most $O(n)$ such writes occur per sweep, hence $O(n^2)$ in total. Each stage then makes a fixed number of recurrence calls. Unavailable coefficient/evaluator results only stop certificate bookkeeping. The reductions, sweeps, exact certificates, transforms, block sums and fixed-size solves contribute $O(n^3)$, and step 1.4 supplies the complete control contribution. Let $q(p)=c^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp$ on $\mathbb R^n$, where $B=B^T$ is positive
definite. Let the feasible set be the nonempty polyhedron
$$C=\{p:Ap=b,\ G_ip+d_i\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\},$$
where the equality rows of $A$ are linearly independent (zero rows are
allowed). Then $q$ has a unique minimizer $p_*$. There are equality
multipliers $\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda_i\ge0$ such that
$$Bp_*+c+A^T\nu+\sum_i\lambda_iG_i^T=0, \qquad \lambda_i(G_ip_*+d_i)=0.$$
They can be chosen so that the equality rows and the active inequality rows
with $\lambda_i>0$ are linearly independent. This KKT tuple certifies the
global minimizer.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,
and let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite on
$\ker A$: $z^THz>0$ whenever $0\ne z\in\ker A$. Then
$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$
is nonsingular. Here the zero-row case $r=0$ is allowed.

Input an SQP subproblem from [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]],
using exact real arithmetic. First reduce the linearized equality system

lexicographically first maximal independent set $E$ of equality row indices
with their right-hand sides. If it is inconsistent, return
`QP-infeasible`.

For each subset $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in increasing bit-mask order:

1. Stack the retained equality rows and the inequality rows $G_i$ for $i\in J$.

   selected inequality multiplier is negative. Otherwise store $(p,\eta,J)$.

Let $q(p)=c^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp$ on $\mathbb R^n$, where $B=B^T$ is positive
definite. Let the feasible set be the nonempty polyhedron
$$C=\{p:Ap=b,\ G_ip+d_i\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\},$$
where the equality rows of $A$ are linearly independent (zero rows are
allowed). Then $q$ has a unique minimizer $p_*$. There are equality
multipliers $\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda_i\ge0$ such that
$$Bp_*+c+A^T\nu+\sum_i\lambda_iG_i^T=0, \qquad \lambda_i(G_ip_*+d_i)=0.$$
They can be chosen so that the equality rows and the active inequality rows
with $\lambda_i>0$ are linearly independent. This KKT tuple certifies the
global minimizer.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,
and let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite on
$\ker A$: $z^THz>0$ whenever $0\ne z\in\ker A$. Then
$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$
is nonsingular. Here the zero-row case $r=0$ is allowed.

Input an SQP subproblem from [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]],
using exact real arithmetic. Let $q$ and $m$ be the numbers of equality and
inequality constraints. Put $A^{\rm eq}=Dh(x)$, $b^{\rm eq}=-h(x)$,
$G=Dg(x)$, $d=g(x)$, and $c=\nabla f(x)$, so $G_i=Dg_i(x)$ and
$d_i=g_i(x)$ for $1\le i\le m$. First reduce the linearized equality system
$A^{\rm eq}p=b^{\rm eq}$: test consistency, and, if consistent, retain the
lexicographically first maximal independent set $E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}$
of equality row indices with their right-hand sides. If it is inconsistent,
return `QP-infeasible`. Within each retained row set, use increasing original
indices; an empty row set contributes no rows or right-hand-side entries.

For each subset $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in increasing bit-mask order:

1. Stack the equality rows $(A^{\rm eq})_E$ and the inequality rows $G_J$,
   in that order. If these rows are dependent, skip $J$.
2. Treat the selected inequalities as equalities $G_ip=-d_i$ and solve
   $$\begin{bmatrix}B&A_J^T\\A_J&0\end{bmatrix} \binom{p}{\eta}=\binom{-c}{b_J},$$
   where $A_J=\binom{(A^{\rm eq})_E}{G_J}$ and
   $b_J=\binom{(b^{\rm eq})_E}{-d_J}$. Thus the equality entries of $b_J$
   are $-h_a(x)$ for $a\in E$, followed by $-g_i(x)$ for $i\in J$,
   in the declared row order. The multiplier vector $\eta$ is stored in this
   same order. The KKT matrix is
   nonsingular by [[lem-sqp-kkt-matrix-nonsingularity-under-reduced-curvature]].
3. Discard the candidate if any linearized inequality is violated or any
   selected inequality multiplier is negative. Otherwise store $(p,\eta,J)$.

If no candidate is stored, return `QP-infeasible`. Otherwise return the
stored candidate with least quadratic objective, breaking an exact tie by the
least subset bit mask, as `solution(p, nu, lambda, E, J)`. Here $\nu$ is
the full equality-multiplier vector, initialized to zero and filled from the
equality components of $\eta$ at indices $E$; $\lambda$ is the full
inequality-multiplier vector, initialized to zero and filled from the selected
components at indices $J$. A finite-precision
implementation that cannot complete a rank test or solve must return
`numerical-failure`; this definition's exact-arithmetic branch has no such
failure. It requires no
feasible initial step and specifies no pivoting rule for an iterative working
set solver.
